chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mundhir, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'We rent out these Kurds in the pastures of the sheep, and they are essentially fire-worshippers, and similar to that. So when the grazing cattle (or the share of the animal) falls to them, they slaughter it and sell it.' He said: 'I do not like you to do that in your property. Indeed, the slaughtered animal is just a name, and one cannot trust the name except from a Muslim.'

key_terms.الْأَكْرَادَ: The Kurds, a specific ethnic group mentioned in the hadith
key_terms.الْعَارِضَةُ: The grazing share or portion of the animal that falls to the renter
key_terms.الْمُسْلِمُ: The Muslim, whose reliability is trusted for religious acts
key_terms.عَبَدَةُ النَّيرَانِ: Fire-worshippers, referring to their religious practice

ai.seo_question: Are the slaughtered animals of fire-worshipping Kurds considered halal for Muslims to eat?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the ruling on meat slaughtered by non-Muslims, specifically the Kurds, who were known as fire-worshippers. He explains that the term 'slaughtered' (dhabihah) is merely a label, and its validity is contingent upon the reliability of the slaughterer, which is guaranteed only for a Muslim. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly view that the religious identity and trustworthiness of the slaughterer are essential for the meat to be considered halal.
